To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the probabilistic projections are a valuable complement to deterministic projections; (b) the probabilistic approach can be used to produce a wide variety of population projections, including those that are not possible using deterministic projections; (c) the probabilistic population projection approach is a useful tool for exploring uncertainty and for assessing the sensitivity of population projections to assumptions about fertility and life expectancy; (d) the probabilistic method is computationally efficient;

probabilistic projections of the future age and sex structure of the world's population are feasible and can be produced for all countries, and can be used to provide a more complete picture of uncertainty than traditional deterministic projections.

probabilistic population projections can be produced by using a combination of probabilistic projections of life expectancy and total fertility rates, and a probabilistic projection of the population at the start of the projection period, with the latter being produced by a Bayesian hierarchical model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of probabilistic population projections, and the R package bayesPop implements these.

the development and application of probabilistic models for projecting population size, structure, and age-specific mortality and fertility rates, as well the numbers of births and death, and derived population indicators, such as median age and old age dependency ratio, using data from the United Nations Population Division and other sources.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the uncertainty in the future population size and structure of countries, and of groups of countries, is often much larger than the official projections imply.
probabilistic population projections should be produced routinely, as they provide more information about future populations than do deterministic ones.
it is possible to produce probabilistic population projections which are more informative than the official ones, while being computationally efficient.
